title: Jeremiah 4:19–31
context: The voice of 4:19–21 cries “My anguish, my anguish!” at the sound of the trumpet and the destruction of tents and curtains. Many readers hear Jeremiah himself grieving for his people; some hear personified Jerusalem, and some hear the LORD’s own grief through the prophet. The text does not settle this, and the notes leave it open. In 4:22 the LORD speaks: “my people are foolish. They don’t know me.” In 4:23–26 Jeremiah describes a vision: the earth “waste and void,” the heavens without light, the mountains trembling, no man, the birds fled, and the fruitful field a wilderness. This echoes the language of Genesis 1:2 (where WEB has “formless and empty”), as if creation were being undone. It is prophetic lament and judgment poetry about the land, not a science text, and the site does not use it to settle questions about creation or the age of the earth. In 4:27–28 the LORD declares the land will be a desolation, “yet I will not make a full end” (compare 5:10, 18), and that he has planned it and will not turn back. In 4:29–31 the cities flee from horsemen and archers, Zion is pictured dressing up in vain before lovers who now seek her life (commonly read as foreign allies, compare 2:36), and the daughter of Zion cries out like a woman in labor. The imagery stays sober and non-graphic. On the LORD saying he has not repented (4:28), the site’s existing discussions at 1 Samuel 15:29 and Jonah 3:10 cover the question of divine relenting and are not repeated here.

verses.text: My anguish, my anguish! I am pained at my very heart! My heart trembles within me. I can’t hold my peace, because you have heard, O my soul, the sound of the trumpet, the alarm of war.
verses.arminianNotes: The voice cries “My anguish, my anguish!” at the trumpet and alarm of war. Many readers hear Jeremiah grieving for his people. Arminian readers see in the prophet’s anguish a reflection of God’s own sorrow over judgment he does not delight in, a heart that longs for the people’s turning even as disaster comes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the prophet’s compassion and note that faithful ministry speaks judgment with tears, not detachment (compare 9:1). Some hear personified Jerusalem instead. Shared ground: both traditions read the anguish as real, both leave the exact speaker somewhat open, and both see grief as fitting for one who speaks God’s word.

verses.text: Destruction on destruction is decreed, for the whole land is laid waste. Suddenly my tents are destroyed, and my curtains gone in a moment.
verses.arminianNotes: Destruction upon destruction, the land laid waste, tents and curtains gone in a moment. Arminian readers see the suddenness of loss as a warning that delayed repentance can find the door closed, and the domestic images of tents as a reminder that judgment reaches ordinary homes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see “decreed” destruction as falling within God’s ordained judgment while the people remain responsible for the sins that brought it. Shared ground: both traditions read the tents and curtains as images of homes, perhaps recalling Israel’s pastoral past, and both hear deep personal loss in “my tents.”

verses.text: How long will I see the standard and hear the sound of the trumpet?
verses.arminianNotes: “How long will I see the standard and hear the sound of the trumpet?” Arminian readers hear the honest lament of one who suffers with his people, a question addressed to God that models faithful complaint and assumes God is listening and responsive.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the same honest question, and note that lament does not deny God’s rule but appeals to it, trusting him even when his timing is hidden (compare Psalm 13:1). Shared ground: both traditions treat “how long” as faithful lament, and both see the repeated trumpet and standard as signs of ongoing war.

verses.text: “For my people are foolish. They don’t know me. They are foolish children, and they have no understanding. They are skillful in doing evil, but they don’t know how to do good.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD speaks: “my people are foolish. They don’t know me … skillful in doing evil, but they don’t know how to do good.” Arminian readers see willful ignorance: the people have not taken up the knowledge God offered, and their skill in evil is a learned, chosen habit for which they are accountable.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as a diagnosis of moral inability: the people cannot do good apart from grace, though they are fully responsible (compare 13:23). Shared ground: both traditions hold that not knowing the LORD is the root of Judah’s folly, and both read “my people” as covenant love that still claims them.

verses.text: I saw the earth and, behold, it was waste and void, and the heavens, and they had no light.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah sees the earth “waste and void” and the heavens without light, echoing Genesis 1:2 (where WEB has “formless and empty”). Arminian readers see poetic de-creation, judgment so severe that it is as if the ordered world returned to formlessness, and they read it as prophetic lament, not as a statement about how creation began.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also read the vision as the Creator’s judgment pictured as undoing creation, underscoring that the one who made the world rules it. They do not use the verse to settle questions of cosmology. Shared ground: both traditions read 4:23 as a vision of the land’s devastation in the language of Genesis 1:2, not a science text.

verses.text: I saw the mountains, and behold, they trembled, and all the hills moved back and forth.
verses.arminianNotes: The mountains tremble and the hills move back and forth. Arminian readers see the shaking of what seems most stable as a vivid picture of how sin unsettles everything, and a call to find security only in the LORD rather than in the land or its defenses.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the trembling of the mountains as a familiar sign of God’s presence in judgment (compare Psalm 18:7; Nahum 1:5), stressing his majesty over creation. Shared ground: both traditions read the imagery as poetic vision rather than literal geology, and both see it as part of the de-creation sequence.

verses.text: I saw, and behold, there was no man, and all the birds of the sky had fled.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah sees no man, and all the birds of the sky fled. Arminian readers note the reversal of creation: humanity and the birds of the creation days are gone, a picture of the land emptied by judgment that calls the living to repent while they can.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the empty land as the outcome of covenant curse, with the absence of birds heightening the desolation (compare 9:10). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as vision poetry about the devastated land, not a claim of total extinction, and both see it set against creation’s fullness.

verses.text: I saw, and behold, the fruitful field was a wilderness, and all its cities were broken down at the presence of the LORD, before his fierce anger.
verses.arminianNotes: The fruitful field becomes a wilderness and the cities are broken down “at the presence of the LORD, before his fierce anger.” Arminian readers see the cause made explicit: the desolation is a moral judgment, not a natural disaster, and it follows from the people’s persistent rejection of God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD’s presence as the decisive cause, the land’s ruin coming from his just anger against sin. Shared ground: both traditions read the vision as the climax of 4:23–26, both hold that the devastation is a response to covenant breaking, and both read the fruitful field turned wilderness as reversing the gift of the land.

verses.text: For the LORD says, “The whole land will be a desolation; yet I will not make a full end.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the whole land will be a desolation, “yet I will not make a full end” (compare 5:10, 18). Arminian readers see mercy within judgment: God limits the destruction, preserving a remnant and leaving room for a future response to his grace.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the limit as God’s faithfulness to his covenant promises, preserving a remnant by his own decision so that his purposes for his people continue. Shared ground: both traditions read “not … a full end” as a real promise of preservation, and both hold that judgment and mercy belong to the same God.

verses.text: For this the earth will mourn, and the heavens above be black, because I have spoken it. I have planned it, and I have not repented, neither will I turn back from it.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the earth will mourn and the heavens be black, for “I have planned it, and I have not repented, neither will I turn back from it.” Arminian readers note that this firm word follows long patience, and that elsewhere God’s relenting is tied to a nation’s turning (18:7–8); the site’s discussions at 1 Samuel 15:29 and Jonah 3:10 cover this.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s settled purpose in judgment, consistent with his unchanging nature, and read texts about relenting as describing his responses within history (see those same discussions). Shared ground: both traditions hold that God’s word is sure, that his judgment here is just, and that mourning creation reflects the gravity of sin.

verses.text: Every city flees for the noise of the horsemen and archers. They go into the thickets and climb up on the rocks. Every city is forsaken, and not a man dwells therein.
verses.arminianNotes: Every city flees from the noise of horsemen and archers, hiding in thickets and on rocks, until no one is left. Arminian readers see the picture of total flight as the outcome warned about in 4:5–6, a consequence that urgent appeals sought to prevent and that the people chose not to avoid.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the scene as the execution of the LORD’s announced judgment, the empty cities confirming the truth of his word through the prophet. Shared ground: both traditions read the horsemen and archers as the invading army, and both see the forsaken cities as covenant curse fulfilled.

verses.text: You, when you are made desolate, what will you do? Though you clothe yourself with scarlet, though you deck yourself with ornaments of gold, though you enlarge your eyes with makeup, you make yourself beautiful in vain. Your lovers despise you. They seek your life.
verses.arminianNotes: Zion, made desolate, clothes herself in scarlet and gold and enlarges her eyes with makeup, but her lovers despise her and seek her life. Arminian readers see the futility of trusting in alliances and appearances, and note that the image, read soberly, exposes reliance on foreign powers instead of the LORD (compare 2:36).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same futility and note how former allies become enemies, a warning that what the heart trusts in place of God will fail it. Shared ground: both traditions read the lovers as nations Judah courted, keep the imagery non-graphic, and see the scene as the end of false hopes.

verses.text: For I have heard a voice as of a woman in travail, the anguish as of her who gives birth to her first child, the voice of the daughter of Zion, who gasps for breath, who spreads her hands, saying, “Woe is me now! For my soul faints before the murderers.”
verses.arminianNotes: The daughter of Zion cries like a woman giving birth to her first child, gasping and spreading her hands: “Woe is me now!” Arminian readers hear the agony of a people facing the results of their choices, and note that the image of labor pain evokes urgency and helplessness in judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the same anguish and note that the image of birth pains is used elsewhere for sudden distress (compare 6:24), where the people themselves speak of pains as of a woman in labor. Shared ground: both traditions read the cry as Zion’s voice, both see the scene as deeply grievous, and both note how the chapter ends in lament.
